Each repeated-outcome analysis runs in three steps: fit the model once, estimate effects from it, then report them as a table and a plot. The names are general (an exposure, a time variable and an optional modifier), so the same functions serve any exposure-by-time analysis, with or without a subgroup.

## Fit mixed model

`fit_mixed_model()` accepts a visit dataset, the outcome column's name and an optional modifier (subgroup) name. Without a modifier it fits visit × arm with a random intercept for each participant; with one, visit × arm × modifier. It returns the fitted model, which the next three functions all use.

What the model's coefficients mean is explained in [Longitudinal data and mixed models](methods_longitudinal.qmd) and [Interactions](methods_interactions.qmd).

```{r}
#| label: fit-mixed-model
#| eval: false
```

## Tabulate model terms

`tabulate_model_terms()` turns a fitted model into a table of its coefficients. `tidy()` makes the model output table-shaped, and `flextable()` formats it. [How this code does it](methods_in_this_code.qmd#fitting-and-tables) describes what this table shows and doesn't.

```{r}
#| eval: false
```

## Estimate effects

`estimate_effects()` asks emmeans for the numbers the plot needs, from the fitted model and without refitting: the mean in each visit × arm cell (and subgroup level), the arm effect at each visit within each level, and, with a subgroup, how that effect differs between levels. It returns them as tidy tables. [Effects behind an interaction](methods_stratified_effects.qmd) explains the method.

```{r}
#| label: estimate-effects
#| eval: false
```

## Plot effect trajectories

`plot_effect_trajectories()` draws the data and those estimates: individual trajectories, estimated means, confidence intervals, numbers observed and p-value annotations. It fits nothing. With a subgroup, it draws one panel per level, each with that level's participants, and a row of p values for the difference between levels. Read it in that order: p-value labels, counts joined to the means, then the drawing layers. For general guidance on writing and reading reusable recipes, see the Functions chapter in [R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) [@r4ds2].
